newsitem.title: MALTA: Malta waits at election crossroads to Europe.
newsitem.headline: Malta waits at election crossroads to Europe.

text.p: Officials in Malta began counting the votes early on Sunday from a general election which could settle whether the Mediterranean island state pursues its efforts to join the European Union.
The opposition Labour Party campaigned on the platform that, if victorious, it would scrap the ruling Nationalist Party's existing application for EU membership..
A final election result was not expected until late on Sunday or early on Monday, despite the small electorate of 275,000 and repeated complaints about the slowness of the vote count.

Reflecting the intimate nature of Malta, where only about 5,000 votes has separated the two main parties in the past, election manifestos covered international and very local issues. But the focus was on the EU and its impact on the lcoal economy.
Prime Minister Edward Fenech Adami, 62, who had a three-seat majority in the outgoing 65-member parliament, pledged to pursue the membership application he made in 1990.
He told Reuters on the eve of polling that he already had a mandate but the election would be a sort of another referendum on Malta's membership of the EU.
Fenech Adami regards the EU talks as complete and says Malta will be ready for membership by mid-1998. Europe "is the only way Malta can go, in our own best interests," he said.
Labour's Alfred Sant, 48, campaigned against membership. He said Value Added Tax (VAT) was imposed on Malta purely to please the EU, pushing up living costs and bringing hardship to ordinary people.
Labour said it would seek a special relationship with the EU while pursuing a policy of "positive neutrality."
Sant also told Reuters that pulling out of NATO's Partnership for Peace programme, which Malta joined in 1995, "will be my first priority."
This would be followed by legislation to abolish VAT and replace it with customs tariffs, undercutting a basis of EU membership and signalling Malta's withdrawal of its application.
No official figures were immediately available on voter turnout in the election. An unofficial count in Gozo, twin island to Malta, put turnout there at 94.6 percent, according to one radio station.

Turnout in the 1992 election, when the Nationalists won a record 13,000-vote majority, totalled 96.04 percent and one electoral officer said: "It's been running about the same as last time as far as one can tell."

Malta has no independent opinion polls and few analysts were prepared to forecast the outcome. But political correspondent Anthony Manduca of the Malta Independent suggested that neither main party would win an absolute majority.

An unknown element was the Alternattiva Demokratikanotes (Democratic Alternative) which won no seats in 1992. It favours EU membership in principle but says a referendum should take a final decision after all conditions are known.
